title: Togo : quand la contestation se heurte au mur du pouvoir
content: The article reports that planned protests on 30 September in Lomé, aimed at opposing the high cost of living, rising electricity tariffs and the shift to a bicameral parliamentary system, were blocked by the Togolese authorities. The protests were organised by the M66 citizen movement, which emerged from the diaspora and gained prominence after the June 6 arrests of rapper Narcisse Essowè Tchalla, known as Aamron. Authorities repeatedly accuse M66 of being a foreign‑orchestrated destabilisation plot. Despite the violent repression on 26‑28 July, the movement has gained notoriety and attracted opposition figures. Brigitte Adjamagbo Johnson, a parliamentarian and opposition leader, called for participation ‘to demand more dignity for the population’. The government cited procedural violations to justify the bans, claiming the marches would disrupt traffic. Organisers had planned a peaceful march in a single file on the capital’s sidewalks. Nevertheless, several activists were prevented from demonstrating: ex‑minister Marguerite Gnakade was blocked at home, and Johnson was surrounded by about thirty gendarmes at her Agbalepedo residence. Johnson said the gendarmes ‘did not allow me to move beyond the barrier’ and that the residence was ‘effectively monitored’, arguing that ‘individual and public freedoms are being violated in Togo’. Aamron reported that when he began marching in a single file, about twenty agents ordered the crowd to disperse and told him to return home, while those accompanying him who did not live in the neighbourhood were also told to leave. The article quotes opposition president Kao Atcholli of the ASSIVITO association, who laments that the leaders ‘think they can govern without the people, driven only by a thirst for power’. The law regulating public demonstrations, known as the ‘Bodjona law’, was adopted in May 2011 and revised in 2019 after the deadly protests against the third presidential term. The revision added a five‑day notification requirement and further restrictions on routes and times, affecting ten articles (3, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 17, 19, 20, 21). The government claims it aims to ‘ensure better regulation of demonstrations and the safety of residents’, but critics say the revision has regressed human‑rights standards. The pastor Edoh Komi of the Martin Luther King movement says the 2019 revision ‘bridged the freedom to demonstrate’. Observers, including lawyer M Célestin Agbogan, argue that the law is ‘liberticide’ and that the UN has recommended its review. Several organisations now demand the complete repeal of these restrictive laws.

title: Togo / 4 Octobre 2025: Grande Manif de la Diaspora en Allemagne contre le régime Gnassingbé - Actualité au Togo | 27avril.com
content: On Saturday, October 4, 2025, the Togolese diaspora in Germany will organize a peaceful march from the Brandenburg Gate to the Bundestag in Berlin to protest the regime of Faure Gnassingbé, according to an announcement published by 27avril.com on October 2, 2025. The demonstration is organized by the Togolese Diaspora Association (DTA), the M66 movement, the MO5 movement, and other diaspora organizations. The organizers aim to denounce 'authoritarian, autocratic, and monarchical deviations' of the regime, citing arbitrary arrests, violence, and the 'monarchization of power' in Togo. The article claims that since June 6, 2025, following the arrest of the artist Essowè TCHALLA (known as AAMRON), the Togolese youth have been indignant against arbitrary arrests, assassinations, and violence attributed to the army and militias of Faure Gnassingbé. The text alleges that these forces use methods 'worthy of the Gestapo and SS,' including kidnappings, torture, disappearances, and forced exile. Regarding the regime's origins, the article states that Faure Gnassingbé came to power in 2005 following a 'massacre of the population,' citing a United Nations report estimating 500 deaths, while other human rights organizations estimate between 800 and 2,000 deaths. The article notes that mobilization has included 'living forces of the country,' religious organizations, unions, and former Defense Minister Essosimna Marguerite GNAKADÉ, who was arrested and placed under custody on September 17, 2025, according to the text. The choice of October 4, 2025, for the Berlin march is intended to commemorate the popular uprising of October 5, 1990, a date when the people demanded democratic opening. The organizers have issued an appeal to national and international media to cover the event.

title: Togo - Manifestation du 30 août : La DMP lance une mobilisation citoyenne -
content: In a press release dated 27 August 2025, the Dynamique pour la Majorité du Peuple (DMP) urged all Togolese citizens to mobilise en masse on Saturday 30 August 2025 across the country. The DMP called for a peaceful march on the streets of every commune and prefecture, demanding a rejection of the constitution adopted on 6 May 2024 and the proposed monarchy, and condemning social injustice, hunger, human‑rights abuses by security forces and militias, and impunity for crimes. The group also demanded the departure of President Faure Gnassingbé and the opening of a new era for Togo. The DMP pledged to march alongside citizens who seek change and a stronger, prosperous nation, while asking security forces to protect citizens’ physical integrity. The article explicitly states, 'Non à la constitution du 6 mai 2024 et à la monarchisation de notre pays,' and 'Oui au départ de Faure Gnassingbé du pouvoir et à l’ouverture d’une nouvelle ère pour le Togo,' illustrating its advocacy stance.

title: Togo – Marche citoyenne du 30 août : le Front « Touche Pas À Ma Constitution » appelle au respect des droits fondamentaux -
content: On August 30, 2025, the front "Touche Pas à Ma Constitution" will hold a peaceful citizen march in Togo. The front urges Togolese authorities to respect constitutional rights and international commitments, to ensure the safety of demonstrators, and to refrain from repression or use of militias. It cites Article 20 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, Article 11 of the African Charter, and the Togolese Constitution. The front warns that since 2019, laws restricting freedoms have been enacted and that UN special rapporteurs have criticized these measures. The front demands full respect for the march, no use of force, security for participants, compliance with international obligations, and no militia deployment. It calls on police, gendarmerie, and military to act with restraint and professionalism. The front expresses solidarity with all Togolese citizens seeking justice, rule of law, and democratic values.  Evidence: 'Le front « Touche Pas A Ma Constitution » appelle solennellement les autorités togolaises...' (the front’s call), 'Le droit de manifester pacifiquement constitue un pilier fondamental...' (reference to international law), and 'Depuis 2019 ces lois liberticides ont été votées...' (statement on legal restrictions).

title: Togo : Faure Gnassingbé nomme un nouveau gouvernement de 27 membres (Liste)
content: On October 8, 2025, Togo announced a new 27-member government under President Faure Gnassingbé, who has been in power since 2005. The new cabinet was unveiled by Secretary General of the Government Stanislas Baba, following the resignation of the previous government on May 2, 2025, ahead of Gnassingbé’s reappointment as head of government. Most outgoing ministers were retained, including Gilbert Bawara, who moved from Public Service Reform to Minister of Relations with Parliament and Institutions, and Robert Dussey, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, known for his panafricanist and anti-imperialist stance, who remains in office. Calixte Batossie Madjoulba, Minister of Security, also retained his position. The announcement comes after protests in Lomé in June and July 2025, during which seven people were killed, sparked by opposition to the 2024 constitutional reform that allows Gnassingbé, aged 59, to remain in power indefinitely as head of government, with the presidency becoming honorary. The protests have since subsided. The new government includes key figures such as Cina Lawson (Minister of Public Service Efficiency and Digital Transformation), Mama Omorou (Minister of National Education), and Pacôme Adjourouvi (Minister of Justice and Human Rights). Ministries of Defense, Civil Service, Social Dialogue, Labor, and Transport are directly attached to the Presidency, according to the official statement.

title: Togo: Manifestation fantôme à Lomé
content: The article reports that the planned protest in Lomé on Saturday did not take place, despite calls from diaspora activists on social media.  The capital remained calm but was placed under high security vigilance, with a large security deployment in several sensitive zones such as Bè, Adakpamé, Déckon, La Colombe de la Paix, and the GTA intersection.  Forces of defense and security were stationed in large numbers at these key points to prevent any escalation.  Most businesses remained closed, especially along major avenues and the main market, and secondary markets were also deserted.  Nevertheless, traffic stayed fluid, with a few taxi‑motors providing minimal mobility.  The night before, citizen groups urged the population not to follow the calls to protest, emphasizing the need to preserve peace and social cohesion.  Activists under the M66 banner, supported behind the scenes by some political parties, hoped to revive street pressure, but their attempt appears to have failed, with the population showing a certain maturity toward such initiatives.  Residents expressed frustration with the economic and social fallout of past tensions, stating, 'Les troubles et les violences ne remplissent pas le panier de la ménagère.'

title: Togo : " appel à manifester, un flop cinglant ", le constat d'u...
content: Activists in the Togolese diaspora had announced a mobilisation for the weekend, but the reality was different: Lomé stayed calm, indicating that the population has largely moved on from repeated calls for protest. Despite a reinforced security presence, no large demonstration took place on Saturday. The slogans launched from abroad met the fatigue of Togolese citizens, who are more concerned with preserving their daily life than engaging in "sterile tensions" (the article). Some businesses closed as a precaution, yet residents mainly expressed a desire to avoid a new economic paralysis, as each lost day further weakens already strained local enterprises and the same families bear the cost (the article). Consequently, the slogans no longer resonate. Togolese people display clear maturity: they reject manipulation and chaos, instead demanding peace, stability and future prospects. The activists’ attempt ended in a resounding failure, revealing a turning point where the streets are no longer the arena for their aspirations (the article).

title: Togo: Entre slogans numériques et réalité du terrain - Le pari incertain du M66
content: The Mouvement du 6 juin (M66) has been urging people to protest on 30 August, presenting the call as a new display of strength.  Activists, active on social media, promise that 'du nord au sud, des villes et villages, la voix du peuple va rugir', yet past attempts in June produced only scattered, low‑impact gatherings.  Online reactions are mixed: some applaud the movement, while many criticize its demands as unrealistic, such as restoring the 1992 constitution, demanding the government’s resignation, or seeking 'liberté totale d’accès à Internet'.  The M66’s strategy highlights the difficulty of the traditional opposition to mobilise on the ground without institutional links or broad party support; these ‘social‑media politicians’ struggle to move beyond the virtual sphere.  The repeated failure of earlier calls shows that the streets of Lomé do not automatically follow slogans posted behind a screen.  In short, the M66’s new appeal to rally on 30 August appears to be a louder virtual force rather than an effective one, with marginal real‑world impact on everyday life.
